# .github/

Three workflows — `workflows/deploy-frontend.yml`, `workflows/deploy-backend.yml` and `workflows/migrate.yml` — plus one composite action, `actions/invoke-migration`, which the last two share. They are themselves the source for what they fire on; read them for the literal triggers. What follows is what they do not say for themselves.

- **`paths-ignore` (frontend) and `paths` (backend) skip a run only when EVERY changed file matches the filter** — a commit touching both a skipped and a live path still runs.
- Frontend fires on push to `dev`/`main`, ignoring `**/*.md`, `docs/**`, `infra/**` and `deploy-backend.yml`: a backend-only or docs-only commit does not rebuild the SPA.
- Backend fires on push to `dev` **and `main`**, matching `infra/**`, `packages/core/**` (the handlers bundle it), `package.json`, `pnpm-lock.yaml` and `.github/**` — the last so a `.github/README.md` commit, which frontend's `**/*.md` ignore skips, still runs a workflow and its gates.
- **The two branches deploy different things.** It is three stacks: the user stack for the ref's environment deploys from either branch, the archive stack from `dev` alone — one archive and one capture serve every environment. So `main` is the only way to reach the prod user stack, and `dev` is the only way to reach the archive; a `workflow_dispatch` on `main` cannot repair the archive. The user stack is deployed FIRST, because the archive deploy is what removes the old migration function.
- Because `main` moves by fast-forward, a release's push range is every commit since the last one, so the prod user stack deploys whenever any of them touched `paths` — and is otherwise left alone, which is correct and worth recognising rather than debugging.
- **A deploy reads back each stack it deployed, because a change set does not count the stack `Description` as a change.** A commit that changes only that text gets back "No updates are to be performed" from `create-change-set`, and `--no-fail-on-empty-changeset` — right for the `.github/**`-only and infra doc-only pushes that reach this workflow with no resource change — reports that as success, so the text an operator reads in the console stays whatever it was. The step after the deploy steps compares each stack's deployed `Description` with the template that ships it and fails the run naming both strings; the repair it prints is `update-stack`, which is not a change set and applies the very body `create-change-set` refuses. Its archive arm hangs off the archive deploy's own outcome rather than a second copy of `!= 'main'`, and the step carries no `if:` of its own — one there would drop the USER arm on `main`. A `Metadata` key and a `Parameters` default are refused the same way; an added `Output` is not, its change set being created rather than refused. A non-ASCII `Description` is refused by `infra/src/stack-split.test.ts` instead: CloudFormation stores `?` for it however intact the template it was given, so no deploy could ever make the check green. The same suite refuses a parameter whose `Default` the deploy never submits: `sam deploy` sends `UsePreviousValue` for every parameter it is not passed, so an edit to that default deploys green and never lands, even in a commit whose change set is not empty.
- **The migration has two callers and one implementation.** `actions/invoke-migration` resolves the runner out of `quirenote-backend-user-<target>`, invokes it in one mode, and holds the three verdicts — a raised handler, an unparseable report, a rehearsal schema that would not drop. It is reached as `$/.github/actions/invoke-migration`: the self-repository prefix, which resolves this repository **at the commit the run is on, with no checkout**, so the apply job keeps the property that nothing from the ref reaches the cluster. The SQL applied is always the deployed bundle's.
- `deploy-backend.yml` ends its deploy job with a `dry-run` and exports the pending count; where that count is not zero, a `migrate` job rehearses on the target cluster and applies. It resolves the same `prod`/`dev` the deploy did, whose branch policy is what refuses a prod migration from another branch. **No reviewer stands in front of it.** One was built — in a `migrate-prod` of its own, because the rule gates a whole environment and `prod` also admits `deploy-frontend.yml` — and removed: the click came before the rehearsal ran, so it carried a statement count and nothing else, and it asked the person who had just fast-forwarded `main` to confirm the release a second time. What replaced it is the `notify` job.
- `migrate.yml` is `workflow_dispatch` only and is the repair path and the bootstrap, not the ordinary route. It takes a `target` with no default, and a `mode` that defaults to the harmless `rehearse` — a `choice` without a default does not open empty, it preselects its first option, so the safe mode is named rather than left to the option order. It resolves the environment `<target>`, so a prod dispatch is refused from any branch but `main` by `prod`'s deployment branch policy, before any credential exists — the same policy that answers for the deploy's apply.
- **The run holds its group until the migration is done, and that is deliberate.** `deploy-backend.yml` groups the WHOLE RUN per branch rather than the deploy job, so the next push cannot `sam deploy` a new handler and new `dist/migrations/*.sql` underneath an apply already running against the old bundle. The cost is that a push arriving mid-migration **waits**. It is not lost: `queue: max` queues up to 100 rather than keeping only the newest pending one, which the default `single` would cancel.
- The apply job also takes `migrate-<target>`, the same group a dispatch takes, and group names are repository-wide, so an apply and a hand dispatch can never meet at one database. That group is `single` — `queue: max` is documented at workflow level only, and an unknown key fails validation for the whole file — so **while one is pending on it, a second entry cancels the first**: dispatch a repair twice and the first is silently dropped. A cancelled run is not a failed one and opens no issue, so check the run list rather than waiting for red.
- **All three jobs that invoke the runner carry `timeout-minutes`** — the deploy job included, since its last step is the plan. The shared action drops the client-side timeout on purpose, so Lambda's 900s ceiling is the only bound and Actions cannot see it: without this a hung invoke would hold the workflow group, and a paid runner, for the six-hour default.
- **A failed apply opens an issue**, and that is what the reviewer was traded for. The `notify` job reads the two jobs' results rather than using `failure()`, which GitHub documents as true "if any ancestor job fails" — `deploy` is an ancestor and runs the whole suite, so `failure()` would file a production-incident issue for a failing unit test. The condition is: the deploy **succeeded**, and the migration did not — `!= success` rather than `== failure`, so a job cancelled while pending on the cluster's group counts too. A failed **plan** is outside it on purpose: it fails `deploy`, no migration is attempted, nothing is half-applied, and a red run is the ordinary signal. One issue per cluster, commented on thereafter, found through the list API rather than search (an index minutes behind a just-created issue) and tolerant of that lookup failing, since `bash -e` would otherwise lose the only durable signal. The body carries the run, the report artifact and a repair that depends on the mode and, for a `rehearse`, on why it failed. SQL the cluster refused must NOT be applied, and neither must a rehearse Lambda timed out, since nothing names what ran long and it may be the SQL. Where the budget refused a statement, that statement and every one after it were never rehearsed, and a rehearsal, replaying the whole history, can never get further; `apply` is what makes progress there, because it resumes off the ledger. Labelled `bug` and `area:infra`; the project auto-adds **every** new issue to Triage, so the labels are for reading, not routing. Its token may write issues and nothing else.
- No workflow here runs on a pull request; the suite runs after the squash-merge and gates the deploy, not the review.
- The two are separate workflows so a broken SPA build never blocks the price capture, and `deploy-backend.yml` runs the whole test suite before any AWS credential exists.
- Frontend's typecheck is inside `pnpm build`, not its own step. Backend runs `pnpm exec tsc --noEmit -p infra` and `pnpm lint` explicitly, because root `tsconfig.json` never includes `infra/` and frontend's `paths-ignore` excludes `infra/**` from ever being linted there.
- Use `pnpm exec`, never bare `npx`, for anything in `infra/` — it declares no TypeScript of its own and resolves it from the root pnpm tree.
- Three dependency ecosystems: root (pnpm), `infra/` (npm), and the pinned Actions (`actions/checkout`, `actions/setup-node`, `actions/upload-artifact`, `aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials`, `aws-actions/setup-sam`) — the last has no manifest or lockfile, so an advisory against one is a hand edit here, **and `actions/` is a second place to edit**: `upload-artifact` is pinned in `actions/invoke-migration/action.yml` and nowhere under `workflows/`. See `docs/reference/DEPENDABOT.md`.

## No dependabot.yml

Never add `.github/dependabot.yml` (nor `.yaml`). GitHub's UI commits this file the moment someone switches version updates on, and `src/dependabot-config.test.ts` fails the suite if it appears. Security alerts and fixes are already on as a repo setting; this file would also turn on routine version-bump PRs, and every merge here costs a review, so version churn would tax the gate for no security gain.

## No README here

GitHub renders `.github/README.md` as the repository landing page in place of the root one, so this folder documents itself as `WORKFLOWS.md` instead. `src/github-landing-page.test.ts` guards against one appearing.
